source.title: On the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Textbooks Need an Update

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error across network widths and depths and reports results that challenge the expected double-descent shape in its tested settings; it also argues that the bias-variance tradeoff is not universal.
record.gate_note: The study reports double-descent curves from other work, but those are cited results and are not rows. It does not measure test error over training epochs or sweep sample size near an interpolation threshold. Several test-error results are presented only in figures, so their values cannot be extracted numerically.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps width and depth of fully connected networks and plots test error, mainly to measure bias and variance. Those curves bear on V1's second descent in over-parameterised networks. The authors call their results consistent with double descent but did not sample densely enough to resolve the peak.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right: the bias-variance tradeoff is not universal, and both bias and variance fall with width. Two corrections are needed. The authors state their Chapter 5 results are consistent with double descent, which they treat as the emerging alternative risk curve. They also say clear double-descent curves are seen in neural networks, and that no single risk-curve shape appears to hold across all models.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures bias, variance, and test error across network widths and depths; it is not a reproduction of the original double-descent intervention or measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: In the small-data width experiment, the reported result depends on tuning the step size for each network size; with a fixed step size, the authors report a U curve in Figure B.7, but do not clearly attribute it specifically to test error. Depth outcomes also differ by architecture and initialization approach: vanilla, skip connections, and dynamical isometry.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report an early hump in variance in some width graphs. They say they 'do seem to see' the double-descent cusp in several variance figures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prediction variance, not only test error, shows a hump near the interpolation threshold as width grows.

record.peer_reviewed: preprint; the text identifies the work as a Master's thesis and the embedded Chapter 5 paper as an ICLR workshop contribution
record.problems: Most test-error curves are figure-only and have no stated numerical values or text description. The width experiments are primarily single-hidden-layer networks, and the depth experiments report architecture-dependent outcomes. The study does not test epoch-wise double descent or a sample-size sweep near interpolation.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying test-error rows were left out.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label was wrong. The study does not report the absence of a peak; it says it did not look for one and that its results are consistent with double descent. This is a thesis and a preprint, and its originals overlap only by citation.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments do not test all deep-network architectures or settings; the width experiments are primarily fully connected single-hidden-layer networks.
The authors state that they did not study how bias and variance change over the course of training.
A small-data setting is included, but the study does not sweep increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold to test whether more data raises test error.
The study discusses double descent in other model classes using cited work but does not test it across model classes itself.
The study discusses effective capacity but does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
The study does not test how label noise or regularization changes double-descent peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
The study does not replot or measure the second descent against an effective parameter count.

rows.value: The text says test error behaves similarly to bias and variance, which both decrease with width.
rows.note: The reported trend does not show the rise and subsequent fall required for double descent.
rows.check: Test error falls with width, matching the over-parameterised second descent. The authors say they were not looking for the cusp, which can need dense width sampling, so a missing peak is unresolved rather than absent. 'absent' overstates this as evidence against V1.

rows.subject: vanilla fully connected networks
rows.size_stated: number of hidden layers varied; 2–10 hidden layers shown
rows.operation_detail: Varied network depth and plotted test error.
rows.value: The text says test error quickly degrades with depth in fairly shallow networks.
rows.note: The reported result does not show a fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: Every depth has zero training error, so all models are past interpolation. Test error rises with depth instead of falling again. The authors attribute this to training pathologies and non-monotone bias, which confounds the result.

rows.subject: fully connected networks with skip connections
rows.size_stated: number of skip connections varied; 0–50 shown
rows.operation_detail: Varied depth using skip connections between every other layer and plotted test error.
rows.value: The text describes a checkmark-shaped test-error curve and says error degrades noticeably at greater depths.
rows.note: A checkmark-shaped curve does not show the claimed second descent.
rows.check: All models interpolate. Test error is checkmark-shaped: it bottoms near 10 skip connections and then rises with depth, the opposite of a second descent. The authors call the confound controls not completely satisfying.

relationships.reason: Past interpolation, extra depth raises test error in vanilla and skip-connection networks and leaves it flat with dynamical isometry (R7–R9). The authors attribute this partly to training confounds.

relation.reason: The study reports its own test-error measurements across network widths and depths, bearing directly on V1.

tranche.reason: The depth experiments qualify V1's model-size generality: interpolating networks show worsening or approximately constant test error as depth increases (R7–R9), rather than continued descent.

source_check.notes: The authors explicitly describe Chapter 5 as consistent with double descent and say their experiments did not target the cusp. Appendix C emphasizes unresolved training confounds in the depth comparisons.
